study.title: Deuteronomy 31 - The succession of Moses, the preservation of the law, and the song as a witness
study.overview: Deuteronomy 31 shows a moment of decisive transition: Moses, at the end of his life, prepares the people to enter the promised land without him. The chapter unites encouragement, leadership continuity, written preservation of the law, periodic public reading and the preparation of a song that functions as a testimony against Israel's future infidelity. The text insists that the life of the people before God depends not only on emotion or memory, but on constant instruction, obedience and remembrance of the promises and warnings of the covenant.

outline.title: Moses encourages the people and transfers leadership to Joshua
outline.explanation: Moses declares that he will not cross the Jordan and present Joshua as the one who goes before the people. The focus is courage based on the active presence of the LORD, who goes ahead, fights for Israel and does not abandon him.

outline.title: The law is written and should be read publicly
outline.explanation: Moses writes the law and the surrender to the priests and the elders, ordering it to be read to all the people every seventh year, in the feast of tabernacles. Reading includes men, women, children and foreigners, to produce fear of the LORD and obedience.

outline.title: God announces the death of Moses and prepares the song of testimony
outline.explanation: The LORD calls Moses and Joshua to the tabernacle, and announces that Moses will die and predict the future unfaithfulness of Israel. In response, it orders a song to remain in the mouth of the people as a witness, remembering both God's goodness and the human tendency to rebellion.

outline.title: The book of law is completed and placed as a witness
outline.explanation: After writing the words of the law, Moses commanded that the book be placed beside the ark as a testimony against Israel. He summons leaders and the people, calls the heavens and the earth as witnesses and closes the delivery of the song to the whole congregation.

study.context: The chapter takes place at the close of Moses" leadership and the imminence of Israel's entry into Canaan. The text itself links the moment to Joshua's succession and to the organization of the people's lives around the written law. There is also reference to the feast of huts and the year of remission, indicating practices already known in Israel and used for the renewal of the memory of the covenant. The setting is solemn: tabernacle, priests, elders, congregation, and the manifest presence of the LORD in cloud.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God's faithfulness does not eliminate human responsibility. The Lord goes before his people, but the people still need to hear, learn, fear and practice. Leadership is received as a vocation granted by God, not as human initiative. The written law has a function of preservation and testimony: it holds the memory of the covenant, confronts sin and calls Israel to obedience. The song ordained by God shows that worship can also serve as a moral and spiritual remembrance; music is not only praise, but an instrument of instruction and accusation against infidelity. The proclamation of hiding from God's face reveals that the rupture of communion brings real discipline, although the text maintains the righteousness of God linked to the guilt of the people, not to a divine failure.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter presents the passage of Moses" covenant authority to the future, and the preservation of the book of the law in a place accessible so that Israel would always remember to submit to the sovereignty of the LORD.
Moses writes the law not only to his generation, but to transmit it to future generations, showing fidelity to the burden received from God.
The hiding from the face of God means withdrawing his approval and protection, that is, to turn away the favorable presence of the LORD in judgment.

questions: Why does the chapter insist so much on public reading, writing and memory, rather than relying only on oral tradition?
How does God's ordained courage in relation to Joshua depend on the divine presence and not human capacity?
The song of testimony challenges our idea of worship: how can the memory of God also confront sin?
study.practice: This chapter calls the Christian community to treat the Word of God as the center of the common life: read it, teach it to children, to preserve it carefully and to let it confront disobedience. It also encourages leaders and churches in times of transition to rest in the faithful presence of God, not in a person's charism. In practice, this can mean establishing regular moments of community biblical reading, clearly transmitting faith to the new generations and cultivating humble courage that obeys even when the future seems uncertain.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not directly inform all the external historical details about the composition of the song, nor does it allow to accurately determine, from this excerpt only, the exact way the reading every seventh year was practiced at all times. The notes provided suggest interpretations of the function of the book and the song, but these readings should be treated as interpretive explanations, not as indisputable statements of the text.
